Configure your server

Apps and clients

Connect the mobile and desktop apps to your server and control push, client updates and what the web app may load.

Connect mobile clients

The iOS and Android app can also point at a self-hosted origin at runtime. On the sign-in screen, tap Use a custom server and enter the same HTTPS origin as WEB_ORIGIN (for example https://app.example.com). Store builds still default to EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL; the in-app setting is an override for people running their own API. Changing the server signs the device out of any previous session.

The app accepts plain http:// only for a private IP, localhost, or a .local name, but Docker Compose publishes the web port on loopback by default. For LAN access, follow Connecting a phone on the same network. A hostname reached over a VPN such as WireGuard or Tailscale needs HTTPS with a certificate the phone trusts, for example a real domain with a Let’s Encrypt certificate issued through a DNS challenge.

Native apps need a setting on the server before they can use its passkeys.

Connecting a phone on the same network

In the Compose stack’s .env, set RAKAZO_WEB_BIND=0.0.0.0 (or the host’s LAN IP), and set WEB_ORIGIN, BETTER_AUTH_URL and API_URL to http://<LAN-IP>:5173. Replace <LAN-IP> with the server’s LAN IP. This publishes only the web port; the API and other ports stay on loopback. For published images, if you changed RAKAZO_WEB_PORT, use that port instead of 5173 in the origins, firewall rule and app address below. The source-build stack uses port 5173.

Recreate the services with docker compose up -d, using the same Compose file and env-file options as your install. Allow TCP port 5173 only from your LAN subnet in the host firewall, then enter http://<LAN-IP>:5173 in the app’s Use a custom server field.

This exposes plain-HTTP sign-in to everyone on the local network. Tailscale or an HTTPS reverse proxy is the safer option.

Mobile push notifications

The API and worker send iOS and Android notifications through Expo’s push service. If the Expo project has enhanced security for push notifications enabled, every send needs an access token; without one Expo rejects all pushes. Create an access token in the Expo account that owns the project and set it for both services:

EXPO_ACCESS_TOKEN=replace-with-your-expo-access-token

Leave it unset when enhanced security is off. A missing or revoked token fails the push with an error that names EXPO_ACCESS_TOKEN; the token itself is never logged.

Mobile incoming calls

Incoming calls ring in the mobile app while it is open. Registered devices also receive an expiring high-priority push: a native call notification on Android, and a time-sensitive notification on iOS. Android uses the existing Expo push setup (including the Firebase configuration in the native build). Android 14 and later may deny full-screen notification access; the call then uses a heads-up notification. Notification permissions and channel settings still apply.

For iOS to ring while locked or backgrounded, optionally configure APNs VoIP delivery on both the API and worker. In Apple Developer, open Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles → Keys, create a key with Apple Push Notifications service (APNs) enabled for the app, and download its .p8 file. Configure these server secrets through your deployment’s normal environment/secret manager:

Setting Value
APNS_VOIP_KEY_ID <APNS_KEY_ID>
APNS_VOIP_TEAM_ID <APPLE_TEAM_ID>
APNS_VOIP_PRIVATE_KEY Contents of the .p8 file; literal \n escapes are accepted
APNS_VOIP_ENVIRONMENT sandbox for development signing, production for TestFlight/App Store (default)
APNS_VOIP_BUNDLE_ID Your iOS bundle identifier; defaults to com.rakazo.app

The adapter uses the <bundle identifier>.voip topic. Keep keys on the server; never put them in the app or repository. Enable Push Notifications and Background Modes (Voice over IP, Audio, and Remote notifications) for the iOS App ID and provisioning profile. The Expo app config declares those modes and the time-sensitive notification capability. Development profiles must use the matching APNs entitlement/environment. Ship a new native build; an over-the-air JavaScript update cannot add these capabilities. PushKit registration is independent of permission for ordinary notifications.

Without APNs configuration, or if APNs delivery fails, iOS falls back to the Expo notification. That fallback cannot provide CallKit ringing when iOS has suspended the app. Every VoIP push is reported immediately to CallKit in native code; an expired push is reported and immediately ended. When the call is answered or declined elsewhere, Android devices get a second push that stops the ring. iOS stops ringing through the open app; a VoIP push would ring again, so a backgrounded iPhone rings until the call expires. Declining from the lock screen uses the authenticated decline endpoint. Its session is kept in the device keychain with access after first unlock, on that device only, so a locked phone can reject the call; sign-out clears it and revokes delivery. Payloads contain only the call ID, bot ID/name, and expiry, never message content or credentials.

Verify locked-screen delivery, answering, declining, token rotation, and multiple-device races on physical iOS and Android devices with the matching push credentials. Simulators and offline unit tests cannot validate APNs delivery or operating-system push throttling.

Client updates

Every web build is named by the UTC time it was built (YYYYMMDDHHMMSS). The web app sends its build on each /rpc request in x-rakazo-client-build (web/20261022093015; the mobile app sends mobile/ and the time its JavaScript bundle was built), and the API answers with the web build in its own image in x-rakazo-build. An open tab that sees a newer build reloads at a safe moment: while hidden, on its next navigation, or after a few idle minutes with nothing typed.

To retire old clients immediately, set RAKAZO_MIN_CLIENT_BUILD on the API, for example web=20261022093015 or web=20261022093015,mobile=20261001000000, and restart it. Older clients get HTTP 426 CLIENT_UPDATE_REQUIRED: the web app reloads, and the mobile app offers its update. Read the current build from the x-rakazo-build header of any /rpc response. Requests that name no build, such as webhooks and API tools, are never refused. A malformed value stops the API from starting rather than being ignored.

Content-Security-Policy

The web server sends a strict Content-Security-Policy: scripts and connections are limited to the app’s own origin. When a CDN in front of the app injects a script, such as an analytics beacon, the browser blocks it until you add its origins. RAKAZO_CSP_SCRIPT_SRC extends script-src and RAKAZO_CSP_CONNECT_SRC extends connect-src. Each takes space-separated https:// origins, with an optional port and leading *. wildcard (https://*.example.com). Keywords such as 'unsafe-inline', bare schemes, *, http:// origins and paths are rejected, and the web server refuses to start until the value is fixed. Restart the web service after changing either one.

For example, Cloudflare Web Analytics loads its script from one host and reports to another:

RAKAZO_CSP_SCRIPT_SRC=https://static.cloudflareinsights.com
RAKAZO_CSP_CONNECT_SRC=https://cloudflareinsights.com

Add only origins you trust: a script these settings allow runs with the signed-in user’s access.

Browsers report what the policy blocks to /api/csp-report. The API writes one csp.violation warning per violation, with the directive, the blocked origin and the page path, so search your logs for it to find the origins to add.

Colors and fonts

RAKAZO_THEME points the web service at a JSON file that overrides the web app’s colors and fonts, including in desktop apps connected to the instance as an Existing instance. Leave it unset to keep the default look. The mobile apps, and the desktop app’s This computer server, keep the default look either way.

{
  "dark": { "background": "#1A1714", "sidebar": "#14110F", "primary": "#E8B26A" },
  "light": { "background": "#FBF7F0", "primary": "#8A4B12" },
  "radius": "6px",
  "fonts": {
    "sans": "Onest, system-ui, sans-serif",
    "mono": "ui-monospace, monospace",
    "files": [{ "family": "Onest", "file": "fonts/Onest.woff2", "weight": "100 900" }]
  }
}

dark and light take any of the color names in packages/ui-tokens/src/index.ts (ColorTokens and WebColorTokens) with a hex value; anything you leave out keeps its default. sans and mono are font-family lists. radius is the base corner size in px or rem (default 0.75rem); smaller and larger corners scale from it. A font that isn’t installed on every device needs its file listed under files (.woff2, .woff, .ttf or .otf, relative to the theme file); the web service serves it from your own domain. The web service re-reads the file on each page load, so a reload shows your edits. Font files must sit inside the theme’s folder. A file it can’t use is skipped with a web.instance_theme_ignored warning naming the problem.

With Docker Compose, mount the folder into the web service:

# docker-compose.override.yml
services:
  web:
    volumes:
      - ./theme:/theme:ro
RAKAZO_THEME=/theme/theme.json

install-images.sh layers that override file automatically. Where you run Compose yourself, as in Production deployment, add -f docker-compose.override.yml after the base file, or the web service won’t find the theme and serves the default look.

Menu links

RAKAZO_NAV_LINKS adds items to the account menu that open a page from the same domain inside the web app, such as an internal tool your reverse proxy serves next to WhatEverFi. Set it on the API:

RAKAZO_NAV_LINKS='[{"id":"clients","label":"Clients","path":"/ext/clients/"}]'

Each id is lowercase letters, digits and dashes, and becomes /app/x/<id>. path must start with a single / and must not be under /app, /api, /rpc, /novnc or /health. Route it before the catch-all in your proxy, for example handle /ext/* { reverse_proxy office:8080 } in Caddyfile.prod. A malformed value stops the API from starting.

Pages open sandboxed with an opaque origin, so they cannot read WhatEverFi’s pages or act with the signed-in user’s session; that also blocks their own cookies and storage. Add "trusted": true to a link only for a service you control: a trusted page runs with the signed-in user’s access, like a script allowed by RAKAZO_CSP_SCRIPT_SRC. The page must allow framing by the app (frame-ancestors 'self'). Links appear in the web app only; the desktop and mobile apps hide them.
